WaitCommand does nothing for a set number of milliseconds, then finishes.

Unlike Thread.sleep(), it doesn't freeze the scheduler — other commands keep running while this one waits.

The duration is in milliseconds.

Declare a private DcMotor field.

In initialize(), get "front_left_motor" from hardwareMap.

In initialize(), schedule an InstantCommand that sets motor power to 0.5. Then schedule a WaitCommand with duration 2000. Then schedule an InstantCommand that sets power to 0.0.

Use three separate schedule() calls. Start the OpMode.

All three commands get scheduled at the same time.

The InstantCommands finish on the first tick — so the motor starts and stops in a single tick.

The WaitCommand happily counts down in the background, but it doesn't control the ordering.

To make them run in order, you need SequentialCommandGroup — covered in the upcoming lesson.

Thread.sleep() would freeze the whole robot, stopping telemetry and disabling the stop button.

WaitCommand only delays one command — the scheduler keeps running, and other commands still execute each tick.

But WaitCommand is most powerful inside a SequentialCommandGroup, which you'll learn next.
